om_angle: Trade barriers meant to build domestic supply chains may instead move Chinese-owned capacity into or next to protected markets. That raises the question of whether the policies achieve supply security or mostly reshuffle where plants are located. Firms must weigh tariff avoidance against higher costs abroad, political risk and partner dependence. The exact FT figures and their data source remain unverified. | The tension is in global capacity location, at the cell and materials manufacturing stage. Its drivers are regulatory constraints (tariffs and local-content rules) and policy uncertainty, which favor plants inside or near protected markets such as Morocco or Eastern Europe for Europe. The contrast between European and North American order volumes points to how different the policy regimes are.
research_question: Use tariff-jumping FDI theory as a lens and compare where plants are sited relative to EU versus US barriers, including foreign-entity-of-concern rules. | The gap between Europe's roughly 120 GWh and North America's roughly 5 GWh in storage orders is a puzzle worth unpacking against the two policy regimes. | Joint ventures (e.g., Gotion–VW) versus wholly owned plants offer a governance comparison under regulatory uncertainty.
data_identification: UN Comtrade for battery cell trade flows (HS 8507); announced-plant trackers from Benchmark or BNEF (commercial), with Rhodium Group's public China FDI reports as an alternative.
keywords: tariff circumvention; facility siting; foreign entity of concern; industrial policy; battery storage

headline: Cleveland-Cliffs pushes Burns Harbor blast furnace reline to 2028 on tariff-supported demand after strongest quarter in three years
summary: Cleveland-Cliffs reported Q3 2026 revenue of $5.6B (up 18.5% year over year), net income of $165M versus a $234M loss a year earlier, and adjusted EBITDA of $612M, on 4.2M net tons shipped at an average $1,177 per ton. It moved the relining of the C blast furnace at Burns Harbor, Indiana, from mid-2027 to April 2028, which frees about 500,000 extra net tons of 2027 shipments. It guided to roughly $715M adjusted EBITDA in Q4, possibly more than $4B in 2027 'under prevailing market conditions,' and 2027 capital spending above $1B.
om_angle: Deferring a reline lets the firm capture high tariff-protected margins now, but it stretches an aging furnace and pushes maintenance into a future whose price and tariff environment is uncertain. The 2027 outlook depends on prices and tariffs holding. The trade-off is near-term throughput versus reliability and capital timing risk if protection is reversed. | The decision sits at the capacity maintenance and investment-timing stage of integrated steelmaking. Trade protection raises the opportunity cost of downtime, while policy uncertainty about how long tariffs last makes the timing a real option. Take-or-pay contracts shift part of the demand risk onto buyers.
research_question: Treat maintenance deferral as a real option under tariff uncertainty, and compare it with maintenance scheduling models that hold prices fixed. | Look across producers for whether tariff shocks shift maintenance outages and capital spending timing, as a natural experiment in policy-driven capacity utilization. | The spread of take-or-pay clauses is a contract-design shift worth tracking alongside protection.
data_identification: Earnings call transcripts and SEC 10-Q/10-K filings for outage and capital spending disclosures; USITC DataWeb for steel imports by tariff line before and after Section 232.
keywords: maintenance scheduling; capital expenditure; antidumping duties; long-term supply contracts; industrial policy

headline: Canada puts oil and gas 'Abatement' category on hold in final sustainable finance taxonomy methodology
summary: The Canadian Taxonomy and Transition Planning Council's final Methodology Report confirms 'Green' and 'Transition' categories. It puts on hold the 'Abatement' category proposed in the July 2026 draft, which would have covered near-term emissions cuts in declining high-emitting sectors such as upstream oil and gas. New research on Abatement starts in 2027. The report also tightens the definition of 'green enabling' activities, adopts 'disclose or explain' for the environmental and social safeguards, and rules out partial alignment.
om_angle: Whether to label emissions cuts at fossil assets as 'sustainable' is a trade-off between financing real near-term abatement in hard-to-abate sectors and risking greenwashing and lock-in. The deferral leaves oil and gas issuers and investors unsure how such projects will be classified. The sector timeline also casts doubt on the end-2026 launch. | The problem sits in the classification rules that sit between capital markets and high-emitting firms. Information asymmetry about whether an abatement project extends asset life, combined with the need for interoperability with other countries' taxonomies, makes the boundary contested.
research_question: Treat taxonomy category decisions as classification shocks, comparing them with how the EU taxonomy handled gas and nuclear. | Think about binary alignment (no partial alignment) versus graded labels from a disclosure-design and signaling lens. | Watch whether Canadian energy firms' transition-plan disclosures or green bond issuance change around the 2026–2027 decision points.
data_identification: SEDAR+ filings and green bond issuance records for Canadian energy issuers; CDP responses for transition plans; the Council's methodology report for category definitions.
keywords: voluntary disclosure; regulatory uncertainty; materiality assessment; sustainable finance taxonomy

headline: Humanitarian Aid Management under Corruptible Distribution and Oversight Agents
summary: The paper models humanitarian aid delivery when both the agents distributing aid and the inspectors monitoring them can be corrupted. Spending more on inspectors or rewards cuts misappropriation but draws on the same finite budget that funds aid, so oversight has a direct cost in aid delivered.

headline: Virginia utilities file first public grid-utilization metrics: Dominion's distribution grid averages 41% use as data center congestion warnings surge
summary: Under a new Virginia law, Dominion Energy and Appalachian Power (APCo) filed the first public measures of distribution-grid utilization with the State Corporation Commission (SCC). Dominion reported 41% average annual use (July 2025–2026) and about 80% during rare peak hours. APCo reported 14% annually and 54% at peak. Separately, Dominion's most severe transmission congestion warnings rose from 8 in 2023 to more than 172 so far this year, covering 2,530 hours and concentrated in Loudoun and Prince William counties.
om_angle: The dispute is over how the metrics should be used. Dominion wants them as a screening tool rather than a 'deciding factor' in rejecting spending. It also wants to watch trends for 3–5 years before making any metric binding. Deploy Action argues this conflicts with the law's purpose, that the utilities undervalue distributed resources, and that five years is too long. Measurement choices matter too. Dominion's 'general' metric counts customer solar and storage as capacity, while its 'planning' metric does not. Grid-wide averages can also hide constrained feeders and substations. | The tension sits in distribution and transmission capacity planning, the stage where regulators approve utility capital spending. Utilities know far more about feeder-level conditions than regulators do. Utilities also earn returns on capital, which may bias them toward building over using existing headroom or flexibility. Large data center loads concentrate demand in a few counties, so local constraints can bind even when system-wide utilization is low.
research_question: Think about the gap between 41% average and roughly 80% peak utilization as a peak-load pricing and capacity-sizing problem, and ask what flexible large loads could change. | Utility–regulator information asymmetry and rate-of-return incentives suggest a principal–agent lens on how utilization metrics get defined (general vs. planning). | The jump from 8 to 172+ congestion warnings, concentrated in two counties, could serve as an outcome for studying how localized data center clustering stresses transmission.
data_identification: Virginia SCC docket filings (utilization metrics), EIA-861 utility sales, PJM load and capacity data, and LBNL interconnection queue data.
keywords: data center electricity demand; grid utilization metrics; capacity investment under uncertainty; large-load tariffs; demand response

headline: Memphis council rejects 18-month data center moratorium but passes 135-day pause
summary: On October 20, 2026, after roughly 5.5 hours of debate, the Memphis City Council split 6–6 (one member absent) on Councilor JB Smiley Jr.'s proposed data center moratorium of up to 18 months, so it failed. The council then passed a substitute: a 135-day pause on new data center applications, meant to align with Mayor Paul Young's 90-day impact study ordered in early October. Some sources describe the pause as covering construction rather than applications.
om_angle: The city must balance AI infrastructure investment against local environmental and community impacts. It has to do so before it has impact evidence or a permanent zoning framework. A short pause buys study time but leaves long-run rules unsettled. Some councilors said they received the substitute text at short notice, which raises questions about procedural legitimacy. | The friction arises at local siting and permitting, where land-use authority over large loads sits. Costs such as air, water, noise and grid strain fall on nearby residents, while benefits flow to firms and the wider economy. Regulators lack information on impacts, which is why the rejected plan sought disclosure requirements. Short, uncertain pauses add regulatory uncertainty to developers' siting choices.
research_question: Local moratoria can be studied as regulatory arbitrage: do projects shift to adjacent counties or states, and how fast? | Treat the 135-day pause, a short and explicitly temporary shock, as distinct from an indefinite ban, using real-options models of siting under regulatory uncertainty. | The 6–6 split and the substitute vote are a close-call setting; compare cities that adopted moratoria with those that narrowly did not.
data_identification: Memphis City Council agendas and ordinances, local permit and zoning applications, GDELT news coverage of data center moratoria across US cities, and EIA-860 for new generation tied to large loads.
keywords: facility siting; data center electricity demand; regulatory uncertainty; siting moratorium

headline: LevelTen: solar PPA benchmark rises 4.9% in Q3 2026 as buyers rush ahead of Section 232 tariffs
summary: LevelTen's Q3 2026 index shows its continental 25th-percentile (P25) solar PPA price up 4.9%. Its new Core-Markets P25 benchmark stands at $64.23/MWh, up 6% year over year and 12.7% since Q3 2024. Wind P25 prices were flat for the quarter but up 13.8% year over year and 27.5% since 2024. LevelTen attributes the solar rise mainly to Section 232 tariffs announced in early August and taking effect in December.
om_angle: Corporate renewable buyers and developers must sign long-term contracts while the cost of trade policy is still uncertain. Much of Q3's increase reflects buyers rushing to sign before the tariff start date. Stockpiling modules is not allowed under current rules, and more than half of modules have already been repriced. How far prices will rise once the tariffs take effect is unknown. | Pass-through happens at the procurement link between module importers, developers and offtakers. Tariffs and minimum import prices raise equipment costs, which developers push into PPA strike prices. Uncertainty about timing encourages buyers to sign early, and restrictions on stockpiling limit the usual inventory hedge.
research_question: The gap between announcement (August) and effective date (December) is a classic setting for pre-buy behavior; compare contract timing and volumes before and after. | Use a VPPA portfolio or MDP lens to ask how corporations meeting renewable targets should time procurement when input-cost shocks are anticipated. | Contrast solar (tariff-driven) with wind (permitting-driven) price paths to separate trade effects from other policy frictions.
data_identification: LevelTen PPA Price Index, USITC DataWeb imports of modules and cells by tariff line, the Federal Register notice for the Section 232 action, and LBNL queue data on project timing.
keywords: pre-buy behavior; industrial policy; price floors; power purchase agreements; long-term supply contracts

headline: Apple commits up to $100M to Pennsylvania titanium supplier and expands film deal with Qnity under its US manufacturing program
summary: On October 20, 2026, Apple named new and expanded partners in its American Manufacturing Program (AMP) for the foldable iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro. Apple commits up to $100 million over three years to Perryman Company, a family-owned Pennsylvania titanium producer. Perryman will melt, forge and roll grade 5 titanium with at least 80% recycled content for the Duo's casing. Apple also expanded its partnership with Delaware-based Qnity Electronics for advanced films used in the 18 Pro's variable-aperture camera; no dollar figure was given.
om_angle: Lead firms are shifting parts of their materials and components supply to domestic producers through multiyear funding commitments. This raises questions about the costs, how resilient the new arrangements really are, and how far such deals go beyond signaling to policymakers. Using recycled titanium also ties reshoring to secondary material supply. | The decision sits at upstream materials and components sourcing. Policy uncertainty and concentration risk in offshore supply push buyers toward domestic suppliers. Smaller domestic suppliers, such as a family-owned titanium firm, need guaranteed demand and capital before investing in new capacity, so the buyer commits funding up front.
research_question: Event-study logic applies: how does the market value supplier-level reshoring announcements, and do suppliers react differently from the buyer? | Buyer-funded capacity at small suppliers fits supply-contract and capacity-investment models; think about who bears demand risk over the three years. | A recycled-content requirement in reshored supply is a puzzle for closed-loop supply chain work: where does the scrap come from?
data_identification: Apple newsroom releases and Supplier List, SEC EDGAR 10-K/8-K filings, FactSet Revere links (public alternative: Compustat customer segments), and USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries for titanium.
keywords: supplier diversification; secondary materials; long-term supply contracts; reshoring; industrial policy

headline: USGBC launches TRUE v2 zero-waste certification with reweighted scoring and a 100-point scale
summary: Around October 20, 2026, the US Green Building Council launched TRUE v2 (Total Resource Use and Efficiency), a zero-waste certification for facilities, construction projects and events. The update streamlines requirements, gives more credit to harder, higher-impact actions, rebalances points to help newcomers, and raises maximum points from 81 to 100 (per Facilities Dive). USGBC says the roughly 10-year-old program has more than 680 certified projects that have diverted 8.9 million tons of waste from disposal.
om_angle: Voluntary certifications face a trade-off. Making them easier attracts more adopters but risks diluting their meaning, while rewarding high performers keeps them credible. Changing the point scale and weights also makes v1 and v2 scores hard to compare. It is unclear whether certification produces real waste reductions or mainly documents existing practice. | The friction is in voluntary third-party certification. Outsiders cannot easily verify a facility's waste performance, so certification serves as a signal, and its design decides who adopts and whether a pass reflects real effort. Rising landfill costs change the business case on the adoption side.
research_question: Use a certification-design lens (signaling, isomorphism) to ask whether lowering entry barriers changes the type of adopter. | The v1-to-v2 change is a standard revision that could be studied like ISO version transitions: adoption timing and early-mover effects. | Compare certified projects' reported diversion with local disposal costs to see whether economics or signaling drives adoption.
data_identification: USGBC TRUE certified project directory, EPA materials, waste and recycling facts and figures, and state landfill tipping-fee data.
keywords: zero waste certification; voluntary disclosure; secondary materials; sustainability standards

headline: A Decision-Support Framework for Food Bank Operations: Overcoming Waste and Uncertainty in Food Distribution
summary: The paper develops forward-looking allocation policies for food banks that must distribute uncertain, perishable donations. The policies balance effectiveness (nutrition and freshness relative to need), efficiency (volume distributed and waste avoided) and equity, where myopic rules tend to fall short.

headline: Google expands Voltus deal to roughly 1GW virtual power plant in PJM
summary: On Oct. 22, 2026, Google and Voltus announced a Google-funded virtual power plant (VPP) in the PJM Interconnection region. Utility Dive reports it adds 1,070MW to a 100MW deal signed in June 2026, for roughly 1.17GW in total, which Google calls a "tenfold" expansion. Google describes it as "one of the largest known distributed capacity portfolios deployed by a hyperscaler to date." Financial terms were not disclosed. On duration, DCD reports about three years, but a Voltus spokesperson told Utility Dive the VPP ramps up over three to four years and then runs under contract with Google through 2040.
om_angle: Hyperscalers need firm capacity faster than new generation and transmission can be built. The open question is whether contracted, aggregated demand flexibility from third parties can credibly stand in for physical capacity backing a large new load. Doing so shifts reliability risk onto thousands of small participants whose availability and response are uncertain. | The friction sits at the interconnection and resource-adequacy stage. PJM's capacity shortfall and long queues slow how quickly large loads can connect. A VPP's reliability value depends on participant behavior, fatigue and the accuracy of baseline measurement, which creates information asymmetry between the aggregator, the grid operator and the buyer. Who captures the value of flexibility (Google, Voltus, participants or ratepayers) depends on market rules for demand response in capacity markets.
research_question: Think of the VPP as a portfolio of unreliable small suppliers: models of random yield and supplier diversification may carry over to aggregated demand response. | Compare the economics of contracted flexibility with long-term power purchase agreements: who bears volume risk, and over what horizon (note the conflicting reports on whether the term is about three years or through 2040)? | The 240% jump in PJM demand response revenue alongside data center growth invites a look at how capacity prices drive demand response supply.
data_identification: PJM Data Miner and capacity auction results for demand response cleared and prices; EIA-861 demand response and customer data by utility; FERC eLibrary for PJM demand response rule filings.
keywords: demand response; capacity markets; data center electricity demand; interconnection queues; grid reliability standards

headline: ISSB publishes first exposure draft on nature-related disclosures, open for comment until Feb. 19, 2027
summary: On Oct. 22, 2026, the ISSB released its first exposure draft of nature-related disclosure requirements, framed as a non-mandatory IFRS Practice Statement rather than a standard. It would cover how nature-related risks feed into strategy, how resilient the business model is to them, the amount and percentage of assets or activities exposed, and nature targets including location-specific aspects. Comments are open until Feb. 19, 2027.
om_angle: Biodiversity and ecosystem dependencies are location-specific and usually sit deep in supply chains, so meaningful disclosure requires traceability many firms lack. The consultation itself asks whether nature content should be a voluntary practice statement or a standalone mandatory standard. That leaves firms and investors unsure how much to invest in data systems now. | The friction is in upstream sourcing visibility and the regulatory design of disclosure. Exposure metrics need site-level data on suppliers' locations and practices, which creates multi-tier information asymmetry. A voluntary format adds regulatory uncertainty, and adoption will vary by jurisdiction.
research_question: Jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction adoption of a voluntary statement could create staggered treatment useful for difference-in-differences designs. | Compare with climate disclosure: did scope 3 reporting push firms to map and change suppliers, and would nature metrics do the same? | Event studies around ISSB milestones (draft release, comment deadline, final decision on mandatory status) for firms in nature-dependent sectors.
data_identification: CDP forests and water questionnaires for current nature-related disclosure; SEC EDGAR 10-K text for biodiversity mentions; comment letters posted on the IFRS consultation page.
keywords: nature-related disclosure; biodiversity risk; multi-tier traceability; voluntary disclosure; regulatory uncertainty

headline: Coca-Cola, Nestlé and Danone agree to change EU plastic-bottle recycling claims after consumer-group complaint
summary: On Oct. 22, 2026, the European Commission announced that Coca-Cola, Nestlé and Danone have agreed to change recycling claims on plastic bottles sold in the EU. The agreement followed talks with the Commission and the CPC network of national consumer authorities, reportedly led by Sweden and Hungary. "100% recycled" and "100% recyclable" claims must now say they exclude the cap and label. The firms also agreed not to imply a closed recycling loop or use misleading green imagery.
om_angle: Brand claims about recycled content and recyclability rest on a system the brand does not control. The gap between product-level claims and actual system-level recovery is what regulators challenged. No deadline for the label changes and no penalties were reported, so the commitments' real effect is uncertain. BEUC says it will monitor compliance. | The problem arises at the interface between packaging design and marketing on one side and municipal collection and sorting on the other. Recyclability is a property of the whole reverse supply chain, not the bottle alone. Consumers cannot verify claims, which creates information asymmetry. Enforcement through negotiated commitments rather than fines leaves incentives to comply weak.
research_question: Information economics of credence attributes: when do claim restrictions change packaging design, not just wording? | Staggered timing of the three firms' commitments (June 2025, February 2026, October 2026) might allow before/after comparisons of labels or marketing. | Contrast enforcement through negotiated commitments with deposit return systems or EPR fees as levers on actual recycled content.
data_identification: Mintel GNPD for on-pack claim changes across EU bottle launches; Eurostat packaging waste statistics for national recycling rates; RepRisk or GDELT for greenwashing incident coverage.
keywords: packaging regulation; regulatory enforcement; deposit return systems; secondary materials; greenwashing

headline: Helen of Troy plans to spend part of an expected $80.5M IEEPA tariff refund on clearing inventory and redesigning packaging
summary: Helen of Troy (Hydro Flask, Osprey, Drybar) said on its Oct. 8 earnings call that it expects $80.5M in fiscal 2027 refunds of IEEPA tariffs, which the Supreme Court struck down in February. Its fiscal year ends Feb. 28, 2027. In Q2 it recognized $26.9M in gross pretax refunds, of which about $4M remained as net pretax benefit after offsetting commodity, fuel and freight costs. For the full year it plans to reinvest $66.5M–$70.5M, including clearing slow-moving inventory and redesigning packaging to meet U.S. and foreign environmental laws.
om_angle: A reversed trade policy produces a cash windfall. The firm must decide whether to bank it or redeploy it into operations: writing down or liquidating excess inventory built during the tariff period, and funding packaging redesign driven by environmental regulations. The split between these uses has not been disclosed. | The problem originates in policy uncertainty upstream. Tariffs imposed and then invalidated distorted sourcing and inventory decisions, leaving slow-moving stock. A refund creates slack to fix those distortions. Packaging-related environmental laws (for example, EPR-type rules) add a parallel compliance cost competing for the same funds.
research_question: The refund is a plausibly exogenous cash shock: compare inventory and capex behavior of refund recipients with that of firms that were less exposed to IEEPA tariffs. | A newsvendor or excess-inventory disposal lens: does a windfall change the timing of liquidating stale stock? | Consider how packaging regulations compete with other uses of operating cash across firms.
data_identification: Earnings call transcripts and SEC EDGAR 10-Q filings for refund amounts and stated uses; Compustat inventory and capex; USITC DataWeb for import exposure by tariff line.
keywords: regulatory uncertainty; packaging regulation; extended producer responsibility; tariff refunds; inventory management

headline: Paper and packaging makers pass record diesel costs to customers via surcharges and price increases
summary: After U.S. diesel hit a record high in September, paper and packaging makers have begun adding fuel costs to their prices. Sylvamo added a $1 per hundredweight surcharge from Oct. 1, Sustana $20/ton from Oct. 12, and Billerud $25/ton from Nov. 1. Smurfit Westrock is instead building freight costs into its third containerboard price increase of the year, reported at $100/ton effective Sept. 1. Sonoco says its surcharge "will come and go as diesel varies."
om_angle: Firms must choose how to pass an energy cost shock downstream. A transparent, reversible surcharge tracks diesel prices. A built-in list-price increase may stick after costs fall. The choice affects customer relationships, margin risk and competitive signaling, and it may also push mills to shorten the logistics behind recycled fiber. | The friction is in outbound and inbound freight for heavy, low-value-density goods with no scalable modal alternative. Contract design determines who bears fuel-price volatility. In a concentrated industry, one firm's surcharge announcement (Sylvamo said it expected others to follow) raises questions about coordination and price signaling.
research_question: Compare surcharge versus built-in price increase as contract forms: asymmetric pass-through ("rockets and feathers") is a natural test once diesel falls. | Look at the staggered timing of surcharge announcements across mills through the lens of price leadership or signaling. | Fuel shocks as a driver of localizing recycled-fiber sourcing: a spatial or network model of reverse logistics.
data_identification: EIA weekly retail on-highway diesel prices against mill surcharge announcements; earnings call transcripts for pass-through language; DAT/SONAR truckload rates (public alternative: BTS freight indicators).
keywords: freight rates; chokepoint disruption; cost pass-through; fuel surcharges; secondary materials

headline: EXPRESS: Harnessing Renewable Portfolio Standards for Sustainable Futures: An Empirical Examination of Spillover Effects
summary: This empirical study asks whether state renewable portfolio standards spill over beyond directly regulated firms, to their supply chain partners and peer firms, and so affect their energy use and GHG emissions. It treats this policy spillover as an understudied channel linking public energy rules to firm environmental performance.

headline: EXPRESS: Do You Lose When You Sell Loose? Impact of Unpackaged Sales on Profit and Waste
summary: The paper models a retailer of a highly perishable product choosing between fixed-size packages and loose sales (or both), setting prices and package size to maximize profit. Consumers see loose products as fresher but face an inconvenience cost. It asks whether loose sales, often promoted as waste-reducing, actually reduce waste and how they affect profit.

headline: Umatilla, Oregon declares fiscal emergency over Gov. Kotek's pause on data center permits
summary: The week of Oct 20, 2026, the Umatilla City Council voted 5 of 6 members present to declare a local state of emergency over "the threat of widespread financial loss." The trigger is Gov. Tina Kotek's October directive, which stops Oregon DEQ from issuing new air and water permits for new or expanding data centers until July 2027. The city estimates more than $5 billion in regional investment could be delayed or lost, along with about $6 million in direct city losses, up to $12 million in water infrastructure investments and community-benefit payments, and at least 1,000 construction jobs.
om_angle: The state frames the pause as protecting public health and natural resources. Host communities have built their budgets and water infrastructure around data center payments and say projects could slip by two years or more. The resolution asks Kotek to withdraw or change the directive and calls for an economic impact assessment. It also lets City Manager Dave Stockdale coordinate with other local governments on possible legal action. He questions whether the pause exceeds DEQ's authority, violates the Administrative Procedures Act, or infringes Home Rule. | The friction sits at the environmental permitting stage of capacity siting. Data center developers commit capital, and towns commit infrastructure, under long-lived incentive and community benefit agreements. A state agency can then halt the permitting gate unilaterally. Several features drive the conflict. The state bears environmental and resource externalities while localities capture the tax base. Regulatory uncertainty is high because the pause ends in July 2027 but legislative reform is pending. Local finances are concentrated in a few hyperscale tenants. All loss figures are city projections that have not been independently checked.
research_question: Treat the pause as a dated policy shock. Do planned Oregon projects relocate to neighboring states (e.g., Washington, Idaho), get delayed, or get cancelled? A difference-in-differences design using announced-project trackers could test this. | View the dispute as federal-state-local jurisdictional conflict over a gating permit, and compare it with other siting moratoria. | Consider a real-options model of capacity timing when the regulatory end date is known but a legislative regime change is pending.
data_identification: EIA-861 utility sales for Umatilla-area utilities; Oregon DEQ permit records; county property tax and enterprise zone agreements; state PUC large-load filings; EIA-860 for new generation tied to data centers.
keywords: siting moratorium; regulatory uncertainty; facility siting; data center electricity demand; federal-state jurisdiction

headline: Trump opts for 180 days of trade talks instead of tariffs after wind turbine Section 232 probe
summary: On Oct 22, 2026, Trump signed a proclamation closing the Section 232 investigation into wind turbine imports that Commerce opened in August 2025. Rather than imposing new tariffs, it directs Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and USTR Jamieson Greer to open or continue talks with trading partners and to report progress within 180 days. Existing steel, copper and aluminum tariffs that hit some turbine parts stay in place.
om_angle: Developers and turbine OEMs face an open-ended threat. Trump said other remedies may follow depending on the talks. It is unknown which countries will take part or what happens if talks fail. Firms must decide whether to pull forward imports, qualify domestic or alternative suppliers, or wait. | The uncertainty lands at the procurement and project-scheduling stage for wind projects. Turbines and inverters are long-lead, concentrated imports. Policy is deliberately left contingent on negotiations, with a 180-day clock. Overlapping metals tariffs already raise component costs. The national-security framing, through cybersecurity and radar concerns, adds possible non-tariff restrictions beyond price.
research_question: Look for pre-buy behavior: do turbine and inverter imports spike during the 180-day window compared with the aircraft-probe precedent? | Tariff threat versus realized tariff: model sourcing under a regime-switching tariff process, building on tariff-hedging supplier development models. | Cybersecurity-based sourcing restrictions on inverters may matter more than tariffs. Which components face non-price barriers?
data_identification: USITC DataWeb and Census USA Trade Online imports of wind turbines, nacelles, blades and inverters by HTS line and month; Federal Register proclamation text; EIA-860 planned wind additions and delays; LBNL interconnection queues.

headline: DOE designates helium a critical material amid Hormuz-driven shortage
summary: Around Oct 23, 2026, the Energy Department named helium a critical material, opening more federal financing to helium producers. The announcement came days after a 60 Minutes segment on the shortage. Energy Secretary Chris Wright cited helium's essential role in semiconductors and advanced energy technologies. Helium is the 20th critical material; the previous addition was metallurgical coal in 2025.
om_angle: Supply is geographically concentrated and has no substitutes in key uses. Large domestic production has still not shielded U.S. users from a global chokepoint shock. The designation adds financing, but the amount and timing are unspecified. CBS attributes the timing to its own report, which is unverified. | The disruption originates at a maritime chokepoint and at a single large production site. It spreads through a byproduct commodity whose supply responds weakly to price. Downstream users such as fabs, hospitals and pipeline operators cannot substitute away. Policy responds after the fact, through the critical-material list and financing, rather than through pre-positioned buffers.
research_question: Byproduct economics: how does supply respond to a price spike when helium is co-produced with natural gas or LNG? Compare with other byproduct critical materials. | Use the designation date as an event: do helium-dependent firms change their disclosures or inventory policies? | Use a critical-node or chokepoint network lens to explain why domestic production share understates exposure.
data_identification: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries for helium production and prices; UN Comtrade and Census helium trade flows (Qatar vs. U.S. exports); Federal Register critical materials notice; SEC 10-K risk factors mentioning helium.
keywords: chokepoint disruption; raw material security; industrial policy; supplier concentration

headline: Citizen scientists map North Carolina's confidential industrial poultry farm locations
summary: Three nonprofits — CleanAIRE Carolina, the Rural Empowerment Association for Community Help, and the N.C. Environmental Justice Network — launched the 'E-I-E-I-O No!' project on Zooniverse on July 28, 2026. More than 1,600 volunteers identified farms on NC One Map satellite imagery, and the results are being checked by in-person site visits. So far, six counties have yielded 2,011 hog farms and 2,349 poultry farms.
om_angle: Without location data, regulators and communities cannot attribute pollution or odor to sources, as the misattributed complaint shows. Researchers also cannot link farm density to environmental or health outcomes. The project fills this gap from outside the state system. Whether the full map will be published, and how industry and the state respond, could not be confirmed. | The gap sits at the farm level of integrated meat supply chains. Upstream growers supply processors, but the law exempts poultry CAFOs from permits and shields their locations. This information asymmetry favors producers and integrators over neighbors and regulators. Manure is applied to land far from barns, which spreads impacts and makes attribution harder.
research_question: Treat the crowdsourced map as a new disclosure shock. Does public mapping change complaints, enforcement, or farm expansion? | Chain liability: would processors' reputational exposure grow once supplier farm locations become public? | Compare with hog CAFOs, which are permitted, to examine how disclosure regimes differ within one state.
data_identification: E-I-E-I-O No! Zooniverse farm map; EPA National Response Center complaint records; USDA NASS county poultry inventories; NC One Map imagery; NC DEQ air and water monitoring.
keywords: voluntary disclosure; multi-tier traceability; state environmental policy; regulatory enforcement

headline: Port of Los Angeles reports record-low emissions per container as volumes near 10.2M TEUs
summary: The port's 2025 Inventory of Air Emissions, released Oct 22, 2026, shows its lowest emissions per container on record while it handled nearly 10.2 million TEUs. From 2024 to 2025, diesel particulate matter fell 2%, NOx 4% (the lowest since tracking began in 2005), sulfur oxides 5% and greenhouse gases 3%. Since 2005, diesel particulate matter is down 90%, NOx 72%, sulfur oxides 98% and greenhouse gases only 16%, while container volumes rose 37%.
om_angle: Criteria pollutants have fallen steeply, but greenhouse gases are down only 16% since 2005. Engine standards and fuel rules cut local pollutants without deeply decarbonizing. Zero-emission equipment is still only 14% of the cargo-handling fleet. All figures are self-reported by the port. | Progress comes from regulated, turnover-driven segments such as trucks, harbor craft, and fuel sulfur. Deep GHG cuts require electrifying capital-intensive, long-lived equipment and vessels, much of it owned by terminal operators, carriers and drayage firms rather than the port. This split creates misaligned incentives and slow fleet turnover.
research_question: Decompose the emissions change into scale, mix and technique effects by source category; the GHG versus NOx gap is the puzzle. | Fleet turnover models: what drives the adoption rate of zero-emission cargo-handling equipment among terminal operators? | Compare the Port of Long Beach's inventory, or ports without similar programs, to estimate the effect of the Clean Air Action Plan.
data_identification: Port of LA annual Inventories of Air Emissions (2005–2025); NOAA MarineCadastre AIS vessel tracks for at-berth and transit activity; CARB drayage truck registry; Port of Long Beach emissions inventories for comparison.
keywords: fleet turnover; emissions standards; maritime policy; emissions forecasting

headline: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
summary: The paper asks why simple linear contracts persist in grocery channels and why fixed payments usually flow from suppliers to retailers as slotting fees. A multilateral bargaining model, in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers, generates both patterns through a trade-off in contract choice.

headline: FERC orders grids to connect data centers within 90 days, make them pay their own way, and justify large-load pricing
summary: On a Thursday in June 2026 (likely around June 18; date unconfirmed), the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approved a set of orders meant to speed grid connections for AI data centers. Grids are being pushed to handle hyperscaler connection requests within 90 days, a process that today can take years. Data centers must pay for their own power and be flexible in their consumption, and utilities must disclose the cost of adding major new customers. Grids serving almost two-thirds of the US population must report within 30 days on whether there is enough power for data center demand, and within 60 days must justify or revise their pricing structures for new facilities.
om_angle: The orders try to do two things that pull against each other: connect very large loads quickly, and stop existing ratepayers from carrying the cost of the new generation and transmission those loads require. A 90-day connection target squeezes the time available for studying capacity adequacy and reliability. Requiring data centers to be 'flexible' moves part of the reliability burden onto the customer, but what flexibility means in practice, and how it will be priced, is still unclear. | The friction sits at the interconnection and tariff-design stage between grid operators/utilities and large-load customers. Long, sequential connection studies create a capacity bottleneck. Load forecasts are uncertain because utilities cannot easily tell which data center requests are speculative. Cost allocation creates misaligned incentives, since socialized grid upgrades let data centers avoid the costs they cause. Federal-state jurisdictional overlap adds regulatory uncertainty about who actually sets retail large-load rates.
research_question: The 30- and 60-day compliance filings will reveal how different grid operators interpret 'flexible' large load and cost causation. That cross-sectional variation could be coded and compared. | Model a queue with priority or fast-track service for large loads. Who bears the delay externality, and how does the effect change when customers can submit speculative requests? | Interruptible-load contracts and time-of-use pricing offer a ready model family for designing what 'flexibility' should mean for a data center.
data_identification: FERC eLibrary compliance filings and show-cause responses; LBNL 'Queued Up' and RTO large-load queue data; state PUC large-load tariff dockets; EIA-861 for retail rate effects.
keywords: interconnection policy; large-load tariffs; data center electricity demand; interruptible load; federal-state jurisdiction

headline: SpaceXAI unit faces up to about $6.1M in Mississippi stormwater penalties as NAACP turbine suit survives DOJ dismissal bid
summary: In a quarterly SEC filing (dated October 23, 2026, per DCD), SpaceX disclosed that the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality is seeking penalties of 'up to $25,000 per day' from subsidiary MZX Tech LLC. MDEQ alleges construction began before the sites were covered by the state's Large Construction Stormwater General Permit; estimated exposure is about $6.1 million across three sites. The company says it is cooperating and negotiating a single agreed order. Separately, US District Judge Debra Brown rejected the Justice Department's motion to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit over a gas-fired plant in Southaven, Mississippi, which the NAACP says was built and run without the required permits.
om_angle: Developers racing for AI compute appear to be weighing speed-to-capacity against compliance: building before permits are in place and generating power on site with gas turbines. The roughly $6.1M is a maximum preliminary figure, not a final fine, which raises the question of whether such penalties are large enough to deter. The litigation tests whether national-security and economic arguments can shield fast-built AI infrastructure from citizen enforcement. | The problem arises at the siting and construction stage and in the on-site power decision. Grid power is slow to arrive, which pushes firms toward behind-the-meter gas generation. Permitting timelines lag construction schedules. Per-day penalties capped by statute may be small next to the value of earlier compute capacity, which creates a misaligned incentive. Locating near a state border also splits regulatory oversight across jurisdictions (Tennessee and Mississippi).
research_question: Treat this as a real-options problem: when does the value of starting construction early exceed the expected penalty, given a per-day penalty cap and a probability of detection? | Compare permit-to-construction lags and violation rates for data center projects across neighboring states or on either side of a state border. | SEC filings as an enforcement disclosure channel: do firms disclose environmental notices of violation at different times than local media report them?
data_identification: SEC EDGAR 10-Q environmental contingency disclosures; MDEQ enforcement and stormwater permit records; EPA ECHO enforcement data; EIA-860 for on-site generator entries.
keywords: regulatory enforcement; facility siting; litigation risk; state environmental policy; data center electricity demand

headline: Korean pig farms' use of food-waste feed rises 2.7x in 20 months, prompting calls for a ban over ASF risk
summary: Agriculture Ministry data provided to lawmaker Song Ok-joo for the parliamentary audit, reported October 24, show food-waste feed supplied to pig farms rose from 66.5 tonnes in December 2024 to 176.4 tonnes at the end of August 2026. That is a 165.3% increase, about 2.7 times. The number of farms using it went from 5 to 18, and the number of pigs fed it from 9,279 to 22,204. Song notes that all 18 farms have been inside African swine fever movement-restriction zones in 2025 or 2026, and is pushing for tighter inspection of feed makers; the headline says a ban law is being pursued.
om_angle: Turning food waste into feed is a textbook circular reuse pathway, but it creates a pathway for disease transmission. A coming policy shock, the dog-meat ban, may redirect a waste stream toward pig farms at the same time that the farms using the feed are concentrated in ASF-risk zones. Regulators must choose between conditional use with inspection and an outright ban. | The risk sits at the processing and feed-manufacturing link between waste collection and livestock farms. Farms and inspectors cannot easily verify whether feed was properly heat-treated, an information asymmetry. Cheap feed creates misaligned incentives. When one outlet for a waste stream closes, the stream shifts to another (here, from dog farms to pig farms), which is a coordination failure across policies.
research_question: The 2019 ban, the 2024 re-permission and the 2027 dog-meat ban form a sequence of policy switches. Look for how waste flows and feed volumes reallocate across outlets after each one. | A waste-hierarchy tradeoff with tail risk: compare expected disposal-cost savings against the outbreak externality, which is low-probability but high-loss. | Compare with jurisdictions that ban swill feeding outright, such as the EU, versus those with conditional heat-treatment regimes.
data_identification: Korean Ministry of Agriculture food-waste feed supply statistics (via parliamentary audit releases); ASF outbreak and movement-restriction zone records; national food-waste generation and treatment statistics.
keywords: secondary materials; food safety recalls; regulatory enforcement; biosecurity risk

headline: Unverified: Guinea's proposed 150Mt bauxite export cap looms over aluminium outlook
summary: The original AL Circle Q4'26 outlook could not be retrieved, so its arguments, including anything about US tariffs, are unverified. Related AL Circle coverage seen only in search results says Guinea's proposed 150Mt bauxite export cap could leave the market about 33Mt short. Guinea exported a record 114.8Mt in the first half of 2026, and China's bauxite imports rose 17.5% in that half even though China caps aluminium capacity at 45Mt.
om_angle: A single supplier country dominates a key input for the world's largest aluminium producer and is considering a quantity cap. Downstream refiners face a choice between stockpiling before the cap and diversifying to other bauxite sources, under uncertainty about whether and when the cap applies. | The friction is at the raw-material export stage. Supplier concentration in Guinea, plus policy uncertainty about a resource-nationalist export cap, creates incentives to pre-buy and makes import volumes swing. China's capacity cap limits how much higher input supply can turn into metal.
research_question: The record first-half 2026 exports alongside the reported cap plans look like possible pre-buy behavior ahead of a quantity restriction. That pattern is worth checking in monthly trade data. | Compare with earlier mineral export bans, such as Indonesia's nickel ore ban, to see how importers diversified their sources or stockpiled.
data_identification: UN Comtrade and China customs monthly bauxite imports by origin; USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries for bauxite and aluminium; USITC DataWeb for US aluminium imports under tariffs.
