headline: New SONAR index shows truckload contract renewals running about 13% above prior rates
summary: FreightWaves' new Contract Rate Change Direction index (CRCD.USA) stood at 13.11% on October 22, 2026, up from 3.53% a year earlier. In other words, shippers renewing truckload contracts are paying about 13% more than under the contracts they replaced. Tender rejection rates have averaged close to 13% in recent months after rising above 9% almost a year ago. The separate index of average contract rates actually paid (VCRPM1) suggests the increases are sticking this time.
om_angle: Shippers must decide how to reprice and allocate freight between contract and spot markets as capacity tightens. The 2025 episode shows that agreed contract rates and rates actually paid can diverge. Shippers can move freight to other carriers in their routing guide, and carriers can reject tendered loads, so a headline rate increase may not hold. Carriers' migration to more profitable contracts should ease increases, but slow capacity growth may delay that. | The problem lies in the shipper-carrier procurement relationship. Contracts are incomplete: carriers can reject tenders and shippers can route loads elsewhere. Capacity grows slowly in response to rates, and contract repricing reacts to spot-market tightness with a lag.
research_question: Relational contracting lens: high tender rejections are a form of reneging on a relational contract. When does a rate reset restore compliance? | Exploit the contrast between 2025 and 2026: same kind of contract resets, different follow-through. What market conditions separate increases that stick from those that don't? | Lead-lag dynamics between tender rejections, contract resets and rates actually paid can be modeled with vector autoregressions (VARs) or as a contract-versus-spot portfolio problem.
data_identification: FreightWaves SONAR (CRCD, VCRPM1, tender rejections) or DAT contract and spot rates (commercial); public alternatives are the Cass Freight Index, BLS PPI for truckload, and FMCSA carrier registration data for capacity.
keywords: freight rates; tender rejection; cost pass-through; long-term supply contracts

headline: Northern Virginia's data center load drives 765-kV transmission lines across three states, prompting siting fights far from the demand
summary: CNN reported on Oct. 25, 2026 that new high-voltage lines are planned to address a steep power shortage in Northern Virginia, home to the world's largest concentration of data centers. The main project, Valley Link, is a 765-kV line on 160-foot towers running 260 miles from West Virginia through Virginia into Maryland, with a right-of-way as wide as a 16-lane highway. A second Valley Link segment would run 116 miles from rural central Virginia into Northern Virginia, and together the lines could cross dozens of counties home to more than 1.5 million people.
om_angle: Residents along the routes bear land-use, visual and property costs, while the benefits (power for data centers, tax base) accrue mainly to Loudoun County. Advocates, legal experts and even local officials told CNN residents have almost no means to stop the lines. Per analysts and lobbyists cited by CNN, a federal commission (likely FERC) has historically deferred to power operators' assessments of what transmission is needed. The contested decisions are how much transmission to build, where to route it, and how to allocate its costs and burdens. | The friction sits at the transmission planning and siting stage, between a geographically concentrated new load and dispersed host communities. Several forces drive it. Benefits and burdens are spatially mismatched. Need assessments rely on operators' load forecasts, an information asymmetry. Regulators tend to defer to those forecasts. Federal, state and local authorities overlap, so affected parties have weak veto power. Large-load demand forecasts are uncertain, which creates a risk of over- or under-building long-lived assets.
research_question: Capacity expansion under demand uncertainty with lumpy, irreversible assets: compare the value of committing early to long lines with a staged or flexible build. | Cost-allocation lens: compare 'beneficiary pays' with socialized regional allocation when the load is spatially concentrated. | Puzzle: if local actors cannot block lines, do pushback and delay show up elsewhere, for example in docket duration, route changes or settlement terms?
data_identification: FERC eLibrary transmission filings and state PUC certificate dockets for line need and routing; PJM planning documents and capacity data; EIA-861 for utility sales growth in the affected territories.
keywords: data center electricity demand; facility siting; federal-state jurisdiction; capacity investment under uncertainty; cost pass-through

headline: Saudi Arabia plans to store crude in Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns from H2 2027 as the Hormuz disruption hits Asian supply
summary: On Oct. 26, 2026, Singapore's energy minister Tan See Leng and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman announced a 'joint intent to establish an arrangement' for Saudi crude storage at Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns starting in the second half of 2027. The caverns lie 150 m underground and hold up to 1.47 million cubic meters (about 9 million barrels). The volume, pricing, and whether Singapore gets first right to buy in a shortage were not disclosed.
om_angle: A producer is choosing to pre-position inventory downstream, near customers, rather than hold it at origin behind a chokepoint. Open questions include how much to store, who owns and controls release, and how priority rights in a shortage are priced or traded off against the producer's commercial flexibility. The arrangement is only a statement of intent, so its final terms are uncertain. | The problem arises in the midstream link between Gulf production and Asian refiners, where one maritime chokepoint creates correlated disruption risk. Holding inventory near demand shortens response lead time and hedges the transit risk. The producer and host country have partly misaligned incentives: the host wants guaranteed access in a crisis, while the seller wants to keep the option to sell to the highest bidder.
research_question: Inventory pre-positioning and network design with a chokepoint: the trade-off between holding stock at origin and holding it near demand. | Contract-design lens: treat host-country first-purchase rights as a call option and ask how they should be priced against storage fees. | Compare the terms of the Japan, Korea and Singapore arrangements as a small-sample look at how producer storage deals vary with host bargaining power.
data_identification: UN Comtrade crude flows by origin and destination; JODI oil stock data for Asian importers; AIS-based tanker tracking for flows through Hormuz and into Singapore.
keywords: chokepoint disruption; inventory management; long-term supply contracts; strategic stockpiling

headline: European Parliament backs JOGMEC-style agency that could take equity stakes and stockpile critical minerals
summary: According to the FT, as relayed in a secondhand rewrite, European Parliament lawmakers voted to propose a Critical Raw Materials Centre. The agency could buy stakes in raw materials companies, build EU stockpiles and track supplies across the bloc. It would get €2bn under the next long-term EU budget, an amount its sponsor, MEP Mohammed Chahim, concedes would need private, national and EIB co-funding to succeed. The model is Japan's JOGMEC, and the push follows US moves such as the Pentagon's $400mn, 15% stake in MP Materials with a 10-year $110/kg NdPr price floor.
om_angle: Should the EU move from permitting support to direct state participation (equity stakes, stockpiles and possibly price support) to secure supply? The trade-offs are cost against effectiveness: €2bn alone is seen as too small. There is also a risk of swapping one dependency for another; EIT RawMaterials' Bernd Schäfer warns Europe could become as dependent on US rare earths as it is on China. Member states, including previously sceptical Germany and Spain, must still approve, so the outcome is uncertain. | The friction is at the upstream mining and processing stage. Concentrated foreign supply and price swings that foreign players can manipulate deter private investment in European projects, a market failure from price uncertainty and strategic behavior by dominant suppliers. Coordinating 27 member states and pooling funding adds a collective-action problem.
research_question: Compare instruments: equity stakes, price floors, stockpiles and permitting fast-tracks as alternative ways to de-risk supply; contrast the MP Materials deal with the JOGMEC model. | Strategic stockpile design under a dominant, possibly manipulative supplier, including how stockpile size interacts with the supplier's pricing behavior. | Natural-experiment angle: compare strategic-project firms with and without later public financing once the centre's status is settled.
data_identification: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries and UN Comtrade for EU import concentration by mineral; the EU CRMA strategic projects list for project-level outcomes; SEC EDGAR filings for MP Materials deal terms.
keywords: government equity stakes; raw material security; price floors; industrial policy; supplier concentration

headline: Türkiye's food-waste-to-animal-feed program covers 74 of 81 provinces but runs at under half its capacity
summary: Interior Ministry sources say food waste from public institutions and large catering sites is converted into animal feed in 74 of Türkiye's 81 provinces, with the feed going to stray animals, shelters and designated habitats rather than livestock. Combined daily capacity is 65,352 kg, but actual output is 31,274 kg a day. Seven provinces (Iğdır, Kahramanmaraş, Kırıkkale, Kocaeli, Kütahya, Samsun, Tunceli) have no equipment.
om_angle: Capacity is in place but underused, with output under half of installed capacity, while the government plans to expand into more provinces. The open question is whether the bottleneck is supply of waste, collection logistics, demand at shelters, or plant location. The proposal to divert condemned or insurance-destroyed food also raises safety and quality-control questions. | The gap sits in the reverse-logistics link between dispersed institutional waste generators and processing plants, and between plants and end users at shelters and habitats. Likely frictions include mismatches between waste sources and plant locations, collection costs, uneven waste volumes, and coordination across ministries, municipalities and private hotels and restaurants. Food-safety screening of condemned food adds a regulatory constraint.
research_question: Facility location and capacity sizing for reverse logistics: why might a network sit at about 48% utilization, and is adding plants in new provinces the right next move? | Compare institutional sources (dorms, hospitals, hotels) on waste volume predictability and contamination risk. | Food-safety and biosecurity screening as a constraint when diverting condemned or insurance-destroyed food into feed.
data_identification: Province-level capacity and output figures from the Interior Ministry and Zero Waste Project reports; TurkStat municipal waste statistics.
keywords: food waste valorization; reverse logistics; capacity utilization; zero waste certification; biosecurity risk

headline: Lula wins fourth term as Brazil's timber exports face EU deforestation-rule checks
summary: Lula won Brazil's Oct. 25, 2026 runoff with 51.79% to Flávio Bolsonaro's 48.21%, per the Superior Electoral Court, after trailing in the first round, 47% to 45% per AP. Wood Central reports Amazon deforestation is down 71.2% over four years, the lowest since satellite records began in 1988. It also reports the EU's checks on Brazilian wood under the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) start at the end of the year. Bolsonaro has reportedly refused to concede, and legal challenges over a court-ordered two-hour voting extension are possible.
om_angle: Brazilian timber exporters must show plot-level traceability to keep EU market access, just as political continuity, contested by the losing side, shapes domestic enforcement. EU buyers can invest in verifying Brazilian suppliers or exclude higher-risk regions and suppliers. Strong national deforestation statistics may not translate into supplier-level compliance, especially in the high-deforestation states. | The friction is at the upstream sourcing and verification link between forest origins in states like Pará and Mato Grosso, intermediaries, and EU importers. It stems from information asymmetry about origin, the cost of multi-tier traceability, and regulatory uncertainty from timing, enforcement and the political transition. Buyers face incentives to de-risk by excluding suppliers rather than upgrading them.
research_question: Supplier exclusion versus supplier development under due-diligence regulation: which do buyers choose, and how does regional risk shape the choice? | Event-study or difference-in-differences framing around EUDR enforcement dates, comparing EU-bound with non-EU-bound Brazilian timber flows. | Puzzle: does improving aggregate deforestation reduce firm-level compliance costs, or do the costs stay concentrated in high-risk states?
data_identification: UN Comtrade Brazilian wood exports by destination; INPE PRODES deforestation by state and municipality; Trase commodity supply chain mappings.
keywords: deforestation; multi-tier traceability; regulatory enforcement; sourcing restrictions; regulatory uncertainty

headline: GHG Protocol proposes delaying mandatory hourly matching and deliverability in Scope 2 accounting after weak corporate support
summary: GHG Protocol is revising its Scope 2 standard. It now proposes that companies "should" use a stricter Method 1, which requires hourly matching and deliverability, but "may" keep current rules (Method 2) until an unspecified future date, and must disclose which method they use. In the consultation, only 12% of companies supported hourly matching and 19% supported deliverability. A new consultation is planned for Q2 2027, feeding a joint GHG Protocol–ISO Corporate Standard expected in Q4 2028.
om_angle:
The standard-setter must trade off accuracy against participation. Stricter rules would make renewable claims reflect physical grid impact more closely. But companies warned of these costs:
- Hourly matching could discourage participation in voluntary clean-energy markets (87%).
- Hourly matching would add reporting burden and cost (86%).
- Deliverability would narrow where firms can invest (87%).
- Deliverability could push buyers from long-term contracts toward spot purchases (72%).

The compromise leaves the mandatory date open. Method 1 also becomes required only if data meeting quality criteria exists, which could delay it further. | The friction sits at the measurement rule that turns procurement contracts into reported emissions.
- Firms' incentives are misaligned with the standard's accuracy goal: cheaper annual certificates yield the same claimed reduction.
- Hourly data is often missing, so measurement is costly and depends on data availability.
- The standard is set by consensus among the very firms it governs, which gives them leverage.
- The undefined deadline creates regulatory uncertainty for long-dated PPA decisions.
research_question: Disclosing which method a firm uses creates a self-selection signal. Which firms voluntarily adopt Method 1 early, and does early adoption correlate with existing 24/7 procurement or grid mix? | Contract-portfolio models of corporate renewable targets (VPPAs under uncertainty) could be extended to ask how hourly constraints change the optimal mix of long-term versus spot procurement. | Consultation responses are a form of corporate lobbying. Comparing who objected with firms' location-based versus market-based Scope 2 gap is one angle.
data_identification: CDP climate responses (location- vs market-based Scope 2, instruments used), SBTi dashboard, EIA-930 hourly grid data to build counterfactual hourly-matched emissions, and SEC EDGAR filings for PPA disclosures.
keywords: market-based emissions accounting; sustainability standards; corporate lobbying; power purchase agreements; voluntary disclosure

headline: Anthropic's S-1 discloses roughly $265bn in fixed compute commitments and $417bn in new lease and capacity agreements
summary:
Anthropic filed a 335-page S-1 to list on Nasdaq as ANT. DCD reports three separate commitment figures:
- About $265.6bn in fixed or minimum commitments, with 1–20 year terms.
- About $417bn in future minimum payments under new or amended leases and commercial agreements, mostly for compute. These start in 2026–27 and run up to 20 years.
- An estimated $125–150bn for capacity delivered in 2028–2031.

In H1 2026, revenue rose 1,300% to $16.3bn. The net loss was $80.7bn, of which $72.4bn was a one-off charge, and the operating loss was $693m. (Disclosure: this newsletter is drafted with Claude, an Anthropic model. Figures come from DCD and have not been checked against the filing.)
om_angle:
The firm is locking in decades of fixed capacity while demand is growing fast but highly uncertain. Some agreements have no fixed amount, but the filing says payments are "expected to be significant." This raises three linked questions:
- How much capacity risk is shifted to suppliers, and how much to Anthropic and its future shareholders?
- How are payments structured (escrow, convertible notes)?
- What power, water and climate exposure comes with the capacity? | The friction sits in the upstream capacity market linking AI labs, neocloud and hyperscale providers, and grid or power suppliers.
- Long build lead times and scarce power force commitments years before demand is known. This is classic capacity investment under uncertainty with take-or-pay contracts.
- Suppliers want guaranteed volumes to finance construction.
- The buyer wants flexibility, but has to secure scarce capacity before competitors do.
research_question: Capacity reservation contracts with transfer rights are a lens here. What happens when a buyer over-reserves compute and can resell, or can't? | S-1 and 10-K commitment tables (contractual obligations, lease maturities) across AI firms and hyperscalers could be compared to map who bears capacity risk along the chain. | The ratio of compute-cost growth to revenue growth is a quantified scaling signal worth tracking across filings.
data_identification: The Anthropic S-1 and supplier 10-Ks/8-Ks on SEC EDGAR (purchase obligations, lease footnotes, risk factors), plus earnings call transcripts of named cloud providers; LBNL queue data for the power side.
keywords: capacity investment under uncertainty; long-term supply contracts; data center electricity demand; supplier concentration; capital expenditure

headline: Spain softens draft data center decree: 10 MW threshold, 36-month matching window, but 80% hourly renewable coverage stays
summary:
On October 26, 2026, Spain's energy ministry released a more flexible draft decree on data centers. Changes reported by Reuters:
- The rules now apply only above 10 MW, up from 1 MW.
- New renewable capacity matching each new megawatt can now be built within 36 months before operation, up from 18. Solar has no time limit.
- Renewables must still cover at least 80% of energy in every operating hour.
- A new alternative path allows up to five years to reach 80%, under conditions.

Bloomberg reports a 60% renewable requirement in peak (P1) hours until 2029.
om_angle:
Spain wants to keep attracting investment while ensuring new load is met by new clean supply. The first draft was seen as too strict.
- The higher threshold exempts smaller facilities.
- The longer window and transition path weaken short-run additionality.
- The 80% hourly floor still imposes costly firming, such as storage or overbuilding.

It is unclear how Bloomberg's 60%-until-2029 figure relates to the five-year transition. The full conditions and adoption timing are not reported. | The friction sits at siting and interconnection for large loads.
- Regulators fear that concentrated new demand will raise prices or emissions. Developers face hourly coverage constraints that solar alone cannot meet at night.
- Thresholds and windows create sharp regulatory cutoffs that can distort project size and timing.
- Regulators and investors compete across jurisdictions, which pushes rules toward leniency.
research_question: The jump from 1 MW to 10 MW is a regulatory threshold. Watch for bunching of announced project sizes just below 10 MW, a classic notch design. | Compare Spain with jurisdictions using other large-load rules (moratoria, special tariffs, Scope 2-style hourly matching) as a siting-choice problem. | An 80% hourly floor creates a portfolio design problem: what mix of solar, wind and storage meets the floor at least cost, and how does the solar exemption from the time limit change it?
data_identification: Red Eléctrica (REE) and ENTSO-E hourly generation and demand data, Spanish BOE publication of the decree versions, and project announcement trackers for data center pipelines in Spain.
keywords: regulatory thresholds; facility siting; data center electricity demand; large-load tariffs; corporate lobbying

headline: CANACAR launches indefinite nationwide Mexican trucking strike over cargo theft, violence and toll tax credit changes
summary: On Monday, October 26, 2026, Mexico's freight chamber CANACAR and other trucking groups began an indefinite nationwide strike. Protests were planned in Nuevo Laredo, Reynosa, Monterrey, Tijuana and Mexico City. The Interior Ministry urged talks and said several other transport groups had agreed to negotiate, but CANACAR kept its protest call. Strike duration, participation and border impact were unknown as of Monday.
om_angle:
Carriers are using collective disruption to push the government on security and cost. Shippers and US buyers relying on Mexican production face possible delays at key freight points.
- The strike is indefinite.
- The ministry is negotiating with some transport groups but not CANACAR.
- No figures on trucks involved, delays or economic cost exist yet. | The friction sits at the domestic Mexican trucking link that feeds border crossings.
- Insecurity (theft, extortion) and fiscal changes raise carriers' costs.
- Carriers can't easily pass these costs on, so they turn to collective action.
- This coordination problem between government and fragmented carrier groups becomes a supply shock for cross-border supply chains concentrated at a few crossings.
research_question: Event-study the strike against daily or monthly border crossing counts at Laredo versus less affected ports. Its start date is sharp, but the end date and intensity are uncertain. | Chronic risks such as cargo theft and extortion versus acute strikes: does nearshoring risk show up as an inventory buffer, a route shift, or a mode shift to rail? | Port concentration matters: how exposed are firms whose bills of lading flow almost entirely through Nuevo Laredo?
data_identification: BTS border crossing entry data (truck crossings by port, monthly), BTS TransBorder freight by mode and port, CBP wait-time feeds, and DAT/SONAR cross-border rates (commercial; BTS as a public alternative).
keywords: cross-border trucking; nearshoring logistics; chokepoint disruption; supplier region risk

headline: Shaw Industries runs carpet tile take-back through its outbound distribution network using empty backhauls
summary: Starting in 2022–23, Shaw routed used EcoWorx carpet tile returns through its regional distribution centers. Delivery trucks pick up tile, material from several jobs is combined, and it moves to northwest Georgia on backhauls that would otherwise return empty. In November 2023, the free-pickup minimum (re[TURN] program) fell from 500 to 100 square yards. Shaw now turns 100% of the tile into new backing and says it has reclaimed nearly 1 billion pounds of carpet since 2006.
om_angle:
Returns are dispersed, delayed and small, so collection is costly. Shaw won't share its return rate and calls getting tile back "challenging."
- Returns come most easily where landfill fees are high: California, New York, Massachusetts and Seattle.
- They are harder in Alabama and Mississippi.
- Demolition contractors control disposal and often dump everything together, so Shaw has hired specialists in Seattle, Boston and Dallas.

The cost savings from the backhaul model are not quantified. | The friction sits at the end-of-life collection stage.
- The decision-maker (the demolition contractor) is not the buyer or the manufacturer, so incentives are misaligned.
- Local landfill fees set the outside option, which explains geographic variation.
- Matching returns with forward freight lowers marginal transport cost, but trailer access constraints and small volumes limit coverage.
research_question: Cross-state variation in landfill tipping fees is a natural lens for explaining return rates. Compare high-fee coastal markets with low-fee Southern states. | Vehicle routing with pickups and deliveries (backhaul integration) is a model family for when lowering a minimum pickup size from 500 to 100 sq yd pays off. | Return delays of 7–10 years and uncertain return quantity matter for planning recycled-content inputs in a closed loop.
data_identification: EPA materials, waste and recycling facts and figures (carpet and rug generation and landfill), state EPR reports including California's carpet stewardship program, and state/municipal tipping fee surveys.
keywords: reverse logistics; closed-loop supply chain; extended producer responsibility; secondary materials

headline: Clarios completes purchase of Ecobat's German and Austrian lead-acid recycling sites; reported US deal and $6B figure unverified
summary: The source headline claimed Clarios bought Ecobat's US recycling arm in a $6B deal, but no source confirms a US deal or a $6B figure. What is confirmed: in August 2025, Dallas-based Ecobat agreed to sell its lead-acid battery recycling and specialty lead operations in Freiberg and Braubach (Germany) and Arnoldstein (Austria) to Glendale, Wisconsin-based battery maker Clarios, at an undisclosed price. The EU cleared the deal in April 2026, Clarios completed the purchase in early May 2026, and the formal EU decision was published Oct. 14, 2026.
om_angle: A battery maker is buying the recyclers that supply its secondary lead. This raises questions about who controls scarce scrap feedstock, whether independent battery makers lose access to recycled lead, and whether recyclers are splitting into legacy lead-acid and growth lithium-ion businesses. The garbled headline is also a reminder to check deal coverage before using it as an event. | The friction sits in the reverse-logistics and smelting stage. Scrap battery collection and secondary smelting capacity are lumpy and regionally concentrated. That gives OEMs an incentive to integrate backward and secure feedstock and price stability, and it is why antitrust review was needed. On the seller side, the lead-acid and lithium-ion businesses have different growth and capital needs, which pushes recyclers to divest one or the other.
research_question: Vertical integration into recycling as a feedstock-security move: compare transaction-cost and foreclosure models with closed-loop supply chain models in which the OEM controls returns | Puzzle: why would a recycler sell its mature, cash-generating lead business to fund lithium-ion recycling, whose volumes are still uncertain? | The gap between deal announcement, EU clearance and completion gives event dates to use for studying scrap pricing or competitor responses
data_identification: EU merger decision texts; E-PRTR facility emissions and capacity for European secondary lead smelters; USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (lead) for secondary-production shares; SEC EDGAR filings of US battery peers.
keywords: battery recycling; secondary materials; closed-loop supply chain; vertical integration; raw material security

headline: BNEF raises 10-year US storage forecast 30%, counting on-site data center batteries for the first time
summary: BloombergNEF's Oct. 22, 2026 outlook raises expected US storage installations over the next decade by 30% versus six months earlier. It projects 213.9 GW cumulative by 2030 and 434.4 GW by 2036, despite a 40.9% combined duty on Chinese stationary batteries and rising project costs. On-site data center storage is forecast to jump from 500 MW / 1.4 GWh in 2025 to 4.9 GW / 7.4 GWh in 2026 and 6.3 GW / 8.4 GWh in 2027.
om_angle: Hyperscalers are deciding whether to put storage behind the meter, alongside on-site gas, or to rely on grid-side storage and demand flexibility. These choices shift who pays for capacity and reliability. They are being made under tariff barriers, cost inflation and forecasts that change by 30% in six months. | The problem sits at the capacity-planning link between large loads and the grid. Long interconnection queues and reliability concerns push data centers to build on-site storage and generation. Tariffs on Chinese cells raise costs and add sourcing uncertainty. Tax-credit eligibility shapes whether storage is paired with solar. Because forecasts move this much, utilities, developers and battery suppliers face real demand uncertainty when committing capacity.
research_question: Compare forecast vintages: how much do revisions track announced hyperscaler orders versus policy changes, and what does that mean for capacity investment under uncertainty? | Treat behind-the-meter versus grid-side storage as a make-or-buy decision for flexibility, set against interconnection delay | A virtual power plant (Google/Voltus) and on-site batteries are substitute flexibility strategies; the fact that both are expanding at once is a puzzle worth examining
data_identification: EIA-860 (existing and planned battery units, including co-located), LBNL Queued Up interconnection queues, PJM capacity auction data; BNEF outlooks if accessible through a university.
keywords: battery storage; data center electricity demand; capacity investment under uncertainty; interconnection queues; antidumping duties

headline: European Commission proposes Climate Resilience Law with single reference warming trajectory and mandatory, more frequent risk assessments
summary: On Oct. 27, 2026, the European Commission presented a Climate Resilience Framework built around a proposed European Climate Resilience Law. The law would set one reference global warming trajectory for risk assessments, replace multiple national plans with a single strategic resilience plan, and require better, more frequent climate risk assessments. The Commission estimates about €70B a year is needed for adaptation and says adaptation could return more than 10 times its cost in avoided damage.
om_angle: Physical climate risk is assessed against inconsistent scenarios and plans, so firms, insurers and governments struggle to price and fund adaptation. Requiring a single reference trajectory could change how firms site facilities, choose suppliers and insure assets. But the content and timing are uncertain, and it is unclear whether private capital will actually follow public incentives. | The friction is a coordination and information problem in planning for physical risk. Fragmented national scenarios produce risk estimates that cannot be compared. Adaptation benefits are partly public goods, so private actors underinvest in them. Assessment frequency and the choice of reference trajectory determine which assets look risky. That flows into site selection, inventory buffers and supplier selection in European supply chains.
research_question: A shift from many scenarios to one reference trajectory is a standardization shock; look at the disclosure-comparability literature for analogues | Facility siting and supplier selection under a common hazard map: robust or stochastic facility-location models with climate-dependent disruption probabilities | Compare with how heat exposure hits firm revenues (see R25) to think about which sectors gain most from harmonized assessments
data_identification: CDP climate responses (physical risk and adaptation sections), European Climate Viewer layers, EEA climate-related economic loss data; NOAA Storm Events as a US comparison.
keywords: supplier region risk; facility siting; regulatory uncertainty; climate adaptation; mandatory climate reporting

headline: Mexican trucking groups agree to four rounds of talks with government after strike over cargo theft and extortion
summary: A trucker strike over cargo theft, violent highway robbery, extortion and rising costs began Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. On Tuesday, Oct. 27, Mexico's Interior Ministry (Segob) and the CANACAR, HAMOTAC and FEMATRAC trucking groups agreed to four high-level negotiating sessions on highway security, infrastructure, tax incentives, regulation and operating costs. The size of the strike is disputed: Segob counted 38 protest sites in 19 states with 691 vehicles and 858 participants, while CANACAR said protests reached all 32 states.
om_angle: Insecurity on the roads raises carriers' costs and insurance, and causes losses, delays and now labor action. Shippers and carriers have to choose between absorbing theft risk, rerouting, using escorts or shifting modes. Government responses (security, tax incentives) are under negotiation. Whether this was a one-day shock or the start of a longer pattern remains unclear. | The disruption sits in the over-the-road link of Mexico–US supply chains. Its root cause is a public-goods failure: highway security is under-provided, so the risk falls on fragmented, cost-squeezed carriers. Carriers have little bargaining power with shippers, so collective action aimed at the state is their main lever. Disputed counts of the strike's size also make it hard for shippers to judge how severe the disruption is.
research_question: A short, dated strike gives an event window: look for effects on border crossings and cross-border truck volumes and how long recovery takes | Cargo theft as a chronic disruption versus strikes as acute ones: robustness versus resilience framing (see R32) | Puzzle: how do shippers price and allocate theft risk between carriers, insurers and buffer inventory when security is a public good?
data_identification: BTS border crossing entry data and BTS TransBorder freight data for Mexico-US truck flows; truckload spot rates on Mexico lanes (DAT/SONAR, with BTS as the public alternative); SESNSP crime incidence data on robbery of transport.
keywords: cross-border trucking; nearshoring logistics; driver supply shock; freight rates; labor disruption

headline: RepRisk: companies linked to greenwashing up 28% to 1,594, with energy-transition sectors' share rising to 29%
summary: RepRisk's fifth annual Greenwashing Report, released Oct. 6, 2026 for its July–June report year, links 1,594 companies to greenwashing incidents, up 28% from 1,243. Alternative energy, mining, industrial metals, utilities, and software and computer services made up 29% of incidents, up from 18% in 2022, while oil and gas fell 4.9 points. For the first time, biodiversity links (300, up more than 41% from 216) outnumbered climate, emissions and pollution links (275).
om_angle: Scrutiny is moving from fossil-fuel firms to companies selling transition products and services, including software and computer services, and to nature claims. These firms' environmental claims may be overstated or simply harder to verify. It is unclear whether the rise reflects more misconduct, more scrutiny or measurement artifacts. | The friction is information asymmetry between firms making sustainability claims (product footprints, biodiversity impacts, green finance) and stakeholders who cannot verify them. Operational claims about supply chains and minerals are hard to audit, while media and NGO attention is shifting toward transition sectors. Because incident datasets depend on what gets reported, detection intensity and actual behavior are tangled together.
research_question: Separate detection from behavior: does incident growth track media attention (e.g., GDELT volume) more than operational change? | The rise of biodiversity claims points to nature-related disclosure as the next greenwashing frontier | Gap between disclosure and action: compare the 'glossy green' banks evidence (R46) with RepRisk links for financial firms
data_identification: RepRisk incident data (university access) merged with Compustat/CRSP; GDELT as a public news-volume proxy; CDP responses or SEC EDGAR 10-K text for the claims side.
keywords: greenwashing; biodiversity risk; nature-related disclosure; voluntary disclosure; litigation risk

headline: EXPRESS: Optimal Return Policies with Heterogeneous Search Rewards
summary: The paper studies how an online seller should set its return policy when consumers can do costly research before buying to resolve product-fit uncertainty, and the value of that research differs across consumers. Counterintuitively, full refunds beat no refunds when search is cheap, because the return policy shapes who researches and who buys, not just who returns.
